questions.prompt: Match each test double to its defining role.

pairs.right: Passed to fill a parameter but never used
A working but simplified implementation (e.g., in-memory DB)

questions.explanation: Dummies fill slots, stubs feed canned input, mocks verify calls, and fakes are lightweight real implementations.

questions.prompt: Which double supports behavior verification (checking that the right calls were made)?
questions.explanation: Mocks (and spies) verify interactions — behavior verification. Stubs and fakes support state verification of results.

questions.prompt: A spy differs from a plain stub because it also:

options.text: Records how it was called for later inspection

questions.explanation: A spy is a stub that additionally records the calls it received so the test can inspect them afterward.

questions.prompt: Checking your code's resulting return value or state (rather than which calls it made) is called ____ verification.
questions.explanation: State verification checks the outcome; behavior verification checks the interactions. Stubs/fakes suit the former.

questions.prompt: Which are good guidelines for using test doubles? Select all that apply.

options.text: Prefer the lightest double that does the job
Default to state verification; verify behavior only when the interaction is the point
Always assert only that a method was called, never the result
Use a fake for a stateful collaborator instead of many stubbed calls

questions.explanation: Use the simplest double, prefer checking outcomes, and reach for a fake for stateful collaborators; asserting only 'was called' while ignoring the result lets bugs through.

questions.prompt: Order these doubles by increasing capability/ceremony, from least to most.
questions.explanation: A dummy does nothing, a stub returns canned data, and a mock adds built-in verification of the calls it expects.
